entries.name: Potato
entries.spread: Europe 1500s (Spain), worldwide by 1800; staple of northern Europe
entries.notes: The world's fourth food crop by mass; the origin story of European famine relief and growth.

entries.name: Tomato
entries.spread: Mexico, then Spain/Italy 1500s, worldwide by 1700; large-fruit forms bred in Mexico
entries.notes: Botanical fruit, culinary vegetable; the highest-value vegetable crop on Earth.

entries.name: Onion
entries.wild_ancestor: no certain wild progenitor; likely Allium oschaninii or similar Central Asian species
entries.spread: Egypt and India by 3000 BCE, Greece/Rome, Europe and worldwide medieval onward
entries.notes: The founder allium; keeps for months after curing, so a classic caravan crop.

entries.name: Carrot
entries.spread: West Asia and Europe by 1000 CE; orange form selected in 1600s Netherlands
entries.notes: Purple and yellow forms came first; orange is a Dutch political joke turned vegetable.

entries.name: Cabbage
entries.spread: Greece and Rome, then across temperate Europe; huge in northern cuisine and sauerkraut
entries.notes: Same species as kale, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi and brussels sprouts; the head formed by selection for apical leaves.

entries.name: Lettuce
entries.spread: Greece and Rome, medieval Europe, worldwide 1500s onward
needs: sun to part shade; bolts in heat
entries.notes: Originally grown in Egypt for seed oil; the milky latex gave it its name.

entries.name: Cucumber

domesticated.where: South Asia (India, foothills of the Himalaya)

entries.spread: Egypt and Greece by 2000 BCE, Rome, Europe and worldwide medieval onward
entries.notes: 95 percent water; a shallow-rooted vine that fruits fast with enough warmth.

entries.name: Sweet potato
entries.spread: Polynesia by 1000 CE (pre-Columbus), then via Iberia to Africa and Asia
entries.notes: Storage root, not a tuber, despite the name; reached Polynesia before Europeans arrived in the Americas.

entries.name: Bell pepper
entries.wild_ancestor: wild bird pepper (Capsicum annuum var. glabriusculum)
entries.spread: Spain and Hungary after 1492; sweet type selected in Hungary and the Balkans
entries.notes: Same species as the chili; the sweet blocky fruit is recent breeding, largely Hungarian and European.

entries.name: Garlic
entries.spread: Egypt and India by 3000 BCE, Rome army rations, Europe-wide medieval
entries.notes: Propagated clonally by cloves; the reason ancient armies smelled was garlic as rations and medicine.

entries.name: Eggplant
entries.spread: Persia and the Arab world, Spain and Italy medieval; aubergine in Europe, brinjal in Asia
entries.notes: The only major solanaceous vegetable from the Old World; a nightshade that loves heat.

entries.name: Spinach
entries.wild_ancestor: wild spinach (Spinacia tetrandra or S. turkestanica)
entries.spread: Arab conquest to Spain ~1100, medieval Europe; the industrial-scale leafy green today
needs: short days for best leaf growth
entries.notes: Persian spinach (from Spain) and English spinach (from Arab traders) are the two ancestral morphs.

entries.name: Garden pea
entries.spread: Europe and Egypt by 5000 BCE, India, China; eaten fresh or dried
entries.notes: One of the founder crops of agriculture; Mendel's model plant for heredity.

entries.name: Broccoli
entries.spread: Italy for 2000 years, England 1720 (as 'Italian asparagus'), huge in N. America since 1950
needs: cut before buds open to yellow
entries.notes: A cabbage selected for its flowering stems; 'flowers we never let bloom'.

entries.name: Cauliflower
entries.spread: Cyprus and Italy medieval, Spain via Syria by 1100, England 1600, heat-tolerant Indian types
needs: blanch head by tying leaves over it
entries.notes: The most finicky cole crop; one stress and the curd (inflorescence) never forms properly.

entries.name: Chili pepper
entries.wild_ancestor: wild bird pepper (Capsicum annuum var. glabriusculum)
entries.spread: Portuguese and Spanish ships 1500s; India, Thailand, Sichuan, Hungary (paprika), worldwide
entries.notes: Capsaicin is a bird-dispersed defense: birds carry the seed, mammals feel the burn.

entries.name: Kale
entries.spread: Greece and Rome, then all of northern Europe as the winter green
entries.notes: The original cole crop; the leafy ancestor assumed for everything else in Brassica oleracea.

entries.name: Green bean

domesticated.where: Mesoamerica and the Andes (two independent domestications)

entries.spread: The Columbian exchange: worldwide within a century of 1492
entries.notes: Snap beans; American domesticate that conquered the Old World faster than almost any crop.

entries.name: Pumpkin
entries.spread: Europe after 1492; now the standard autumn lantern and pie fruit
needs: rich soil, lots of space for vines
entries.notes: Third of the Three Sisters (corn, bean, squash); mostly water, pure orange, endlessly carveable.

entries.name: Radish

domesticated.where: Southeast Asia (and cultivated in Egypt by 2500 BCE)

entries.spread: Egypt, Greece and Rome by 500 BCE; worldwide garden crop
needs: cool season; bolts fast in heat
entries.notes: The fastest vegetable; 28 days from seed to plate, the reference quick crop for games.

entries.name: Turnip
entries.wild_ancestor: wild field mustard relative (Brassica rapa subsp. rapa)
entries.spread: Prehistoric in Europe; the medieval and Irish staple before the potato
entries.notes: The original Jack-o'-lantern and the original famine crop; predated the potato by millennia.

entries.name: Beetroot
entries.spread: Leaf beet (chard) by Rome; swollen red root selected in Europe 1500s
entries.notes: Same species as chard and sugar beet; betacyanin makes the kitchen pink.

entries.name: Celery
entries.spread: Greek and Roman gardens; blanched stalk celery selected in Italy 1600s
entries.notes: Grown wild as a bitter herb first; the juicy stalk is a recent Italian selection.

entries.name: Leek
entries.spread: Egypt and Mesopotamia by 2000 BCE, Rome and Britain; the emblem of Wales
needs: rich deep soil; trench planting for blanch
entries.notes: No bulb; the blanched pseudostem is eaten. The Welsh national emblem (worn at St David's Day).

entries.name: Asparagus
entries.spread: Greece and Rome (Cato wrote of it), France and Germany medieval; a luxury perennial
needs: permanent bed; crowns yield for 15-20 years
entries.notes: Perennial; the spears are just aerial shoots racing to the sun. Season is a few weeks, once a year.

entries.name: Brussels sprouts
entries.spread: Belgium 1700s, England 1800s, worldwide temperate
needs: cold sweetens the sprouts; harvest bottom-up
entries.notes: A cabbage selected for axillary buds, each bud a baby cabbage on a tall stalk.

entries.name: Kohlrabi
entries.spread: Central Europe 1500s (German name, 'cabbage turnip'), now global cool-season
entries.notes: A swollen stem, not a root; the original 'space turnip' joke is a thousand years old.

entries.name: Taro

domesticated.where: Southeast Asia and New Guinea (multiple domestications)

entries.spread: Oceania by Lapita voyagers ~ 3300 BP; Africa and the Americas by trade
needs: must be cooked; calcium oxalate crystals
entries.notes: The world's oldest cultivated root crop; the pillar of Hawaiian kalo culture.

entries.name: Cassava
entries.spread: Neotropics by 7000 BP; Portuguese sailors carried it to West Africa 1500s
entries.notes: Half a billion people eat it daily; the quiet calorie king of the tropics, toxic if unprocessed.

entries.name: Yam
entries.wild_ancestor: wild yams (Dioscorea rotundata in Africa, D. alata in Asia)

domesticated.where: West Africa and Southeast Asia (multiple domestications)

entries.spread: West African forests 5000 BP; D. alata via Austronesians to the Pacific
needs: deep fertile soil; mounds or heaps
entries.notes: The true yam; not the American 'yam' (that's sweet potato). Central to West African feasting.

entries.name: Jerusalem artichoke
entries.spread: France and Italy 1600s via Champlain; confusing name, nothing to do with Jerusalem
needs: perennial; dig tubers after frost kills tops
entries.notes: A native sunflower; nutty tuber rich in inulin (the gas question). Invasive if pampered.

entries.name: Globe artichoke
entries.spread: Greeks and Romans, medieval France and Italy; the 'noble' vegetable of Venice
entries.notes: Eat the unopened flower bud and its heart; one of the few perennial vegetables.

entries.name: Florence fennel
entries.spread: Ancient herb; bulb type developed in Italy ~1500s, now staple of Mediterranean cooking
needs: hill up bases to blanch the bulb
entries.notes: The herb is ancient; the aniseed bulb is a Florentine invention. Tastes of licorice.

entries.name: Okra
entries.wild_ancestor: disputed; wild Abelmoschus species of Ethiopia / India
entries.spread: Egypt by 1200, Arab world, then Africa to the Americas via the slave trade
needs: pick pods young or they turn woody
entries.notes: The gumbo thickener; mucilaginous pods, hibiscus's hot cousin, Cajun icon.

entries.name: Bok choy
entries.wild_ancestor: wild field mustard relative (Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis)
entries.spread: China for 1500 years, East/Southeast Asia, now worldwide; the stir-fry green
entries.notes: A non-heading cabbage; the default Cantonese green and the fastest wok vegetable.

entries.name: Rutabaga
entries.wild_ancestor: natural hybrid of cabbage x turnip (Brassica napus var. napobrassica)
entries.spread: Bohemia ~1620, Sweden and Scotland ('neeps'), Scandinavia and Canada
needs: long season, late harvest stored for winter
entries.notes: The other 'swede'; sweeter and yellower than turnip, and the Highland clapshot hero.

entries.name: Daikon
entries.spread: Japan and China for 1500 years; the sushi-deck garnish and pickle radish
needs: deep loose soil for long roots
even water for crisp mild roots
entries.notes: A meter-long radish; in Japan it is the condiment, in winter the staple.

entries.name: Lotus root
entries.spread: China and India for 3000 years; sacred flower whose rhizome is the food
needs: harvest rhizomes after leaves die back
entries.notes: An aquatic rhizome, not a root; slices show the classic wheel of holes. Buddhist icon and snack alike.
